title: Experimental Development - Canadian SR&ED Tax Credit Glossary
description: Read our Canadian SR&ED glossary to learn how Experimental Development qualifies for R&D investment tax credits through technological advancement.
summary: Experimental development is the category of scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) under subsection 248(1) of Canada's Income Tax Act covering work to achieve technological advancement by creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes. It applies to businesses claiming SR&ED in Canada, and the vast majority of corporate industrial claims, including incremental improvements, are filed under it.

body.text: Experimental development is the category of scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) under subsection 248(1) of Canada's Income Tax Act covering work to achieve technological advancement by creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes. It applies to businesses claiming SR&ED in Canada, and the vast majority of corporate industrial claims, including incremental improvements, are filed under it.
Executive Summary and Statutory Architecture of Canadian R&D Taxation

Canada maintains one of the most mature, statutorily intricate, and financially generous research and development (R&D) fiscal incentive regimes among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) jurisdictions. The cornerstone of this federal architecture is the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program, which supports more than 24,160 businesses annually—including over 4,000 claimants in Quebec alone—and operates through a dual-mechanism statutory design codified within the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (Regulation 2900). Rather than functioning as a discretionary grant or ministerial subsidy subject to fixed parliamentary appropriations, the SR&ED program is a statutory entitlement entrenched in federal tax law, jointly overseen by the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates legislative tax policy, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers technical eligibility reviews and financial compliance.

The federal statutory framework delivers two distinct, sequential fiscal benefits to qualifying claimants conducting R&D in Canada. First, under subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers may pool allowable current SR&ED expenditures—and, following the landmark legislative restoration effective December 16, 2024, eligible capital SR&ED expenditures—to deduct them entirely against current-year income from a business, or elect to carry unused expenditure pool balances forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. Second, under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) and section 127.1 of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers earn an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a baseline statutory rate of 15% up to an enhanced rate of 35% on "qualified expenditures". Depending on the corporate classification, prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada, or multi-year average gross revenue of the claimant, these ITCs may be applied to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable, carried back three taxation years, carried forward 20 taxation years, or refunded directly in cash.

Between December 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian SR&ED regime underwent its most consequential legislative modernization since the Jobs and Growth Act, 2012 (Bill C-45) eliminated capital expenditure eligibility and reduced the basic ITC rate from 20% to 15%. Following public consultations initiated under Budget 2024 and formal legislative proposals tabled in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), Parliament enacted Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, with retroactive application to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. There is a vital distinction between the initial FES policy announcement and the final enacted statutory thresholds: whereas the December 16, 2024 FES initially proposed raising the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, the enacted provisions of Bill C-15 ultimately doubled the enhanced expenditure limit to $6,000,000 per taxation year. Concurrently, the legislation expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historical $10,000,000–$50,000,000 corridor to a widened $15,000,000–$75,000,000 corridor, extended eligibility for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to eligible Canadian public corporations via a three-year average financial statement revenue test, and reinstated capital expenditures and shared-use equipment (SUE) to both the subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the subsection 127(9) ITC base.

This structural expansion reflects a deliberate macroeconomic policy pivot by the Department of Finance Canada to counteract capital flight, boost domestic productivity, and retain intellectual property (IP) within Canadian borders amidst intensifying international tax competition. By restoring capital expenditure eligibility and admitting mid-market public corporations to the refundable credit tier, the federal government shifted the SR&ED program from a predominantly early-stage, software-skewed wage subsidy back toward an industrial policy instrument capable of supporting capital-intensive scaling in clean technology, biopharmaceuticals, advanced manufacturing, and artificial intelligence hardware.

body.text: Technical Eligibility Framework and Judicial Precedents
The Statutory Definition Under Subsection 248(1)

Technical eligibility for both federal and provincial R&D tax incentives hinges on the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. The statute defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. To qualify under the Act, the work must be undertaken for one of three primary scientific or technological objectives, or constitute prescribed support work directly linked to those objectives. Under paragraph (a) of the definition, basic research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, whereas paragraph (b) covers applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Paragraph (c) establishes the experimental development category—under which the vast majority of corporate industrial claims are filed—comprising work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Finally, paragraph (d) incorporates prescribed support work with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of basic research, applied research, or experimental development undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Crucially, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes a comprehensive catalogue of routine commercial and engineering activities—even where such activities are technically complex, novel to the specific firm, or financially risky—unless they are absorbed strictly as commensurate support work under paragraph (d). These statutorily excluded activities encompass market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection. Within the software engineering and SaaS sectors, CRA audit guidelines and judicial decisions consistently affirm that routine bug fixes, user interface updates, standard systems configuration, and straightforward adaptations of existing frameworks or APIs do not constitute eligible SR&ED. Rather, software claims must demonstrate non-deterministic development environments, competing system-level architectural constraints, or the creation of novel algorithms that expand underlying computer science capability beyond standard vendor documentation.
Judicial Precedents and the Northwest Hydraulic Framework

Because the Income Tax Act does not statutorily define the phrases "technological advancement," "technological uncertainty," or "systematic investigation," Canadian tax jurisprudence has established the binding legal tests governing SR&ED audits and appeals.
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (1998)

The seminal judicial authority governing SR&ED eligibility in Canada is the decision of Judge Donald Bowman of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC). In Northwest Hydraulic, the Court evaluated physical hydraulic modelling projects and articulated five interrelated legal criteria—universally referred to in Canadian tax practice as the "Five Questions"—that a claimant must satisfy on a balance of probabilities to establish that eligible SR&ED occurred.

First, the Court asked whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Judge Bowman held that "routine engineering" describes techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. If a technical obstacle can be resolved by applying established methodologies, published engineering tables, or standard diagnostic routines, no technological uncertainty exists, even if the specific commercial outcome is initially uncertain to the taxpayer. Second, the Court examined whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty, requiring a structured cognitive and analytical approach that isolates the precise technological bottleneck prior to experimentation. Third, the Court evaluated whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses through systematic observation, measurement, experimental verification, or rigorous mathematical analysis, rather than trial-and-error tinkering or intuitive guesswork.

Fourth, Northwest Hydraulic required that the process result in a technological advancement—defined as an increase in the general stock of technological knowledge or an understanding of why a system behaves as it does under competing constraints, rather than the mere construction of a commercially functional artifact. Importantly, this fourth criterion established the enduring legal principle that a failed experiment fully qualifies for SR&ED tax incentives if it advances technological knowledge by conclusively proving that a hypothesized pathway is scientifically unviable. Fifth, the Court emphasized that a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results achieved should be kept as the work progresses. Although contemporaneous documentation is not an independent statutory condition written into subsection 248(1), it serves as the decisive evidentiary proof during a CRA review or Tax Court appeal that a systematic investigation following the scientific method actually occurred.

In August 2021, the CRA updated its administrative Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives, consolidating its compliance review methodology into two overarching administrative inquiries often termed the "Why" and the "How" requirements. Under this modernized administrative architecture, the "Why" requirement evaluates whether the work was conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement, while the "How" requirement assesses whether the work was a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis to overcome scientific or technological uncertainty. As the CRA explicitly confirms in its historical policy guidance, both the two administrative requirements and the five judicial questions are derived directly from Northwest Hydraulic, which remains the controlling judicial authority in the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6)

In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, the Tax Court of Canada reaffirmed the strict demarcation between custom engineering and eligible experimental development. The corporate taxpayer designed a hydraulic system to control the descent of theatre fire curtains without counterweights and a manual override for automated curtain rigging, and claimed SR&ED credits for resolving project-specific mechanical constraints. The Court dismissed the appeal, emphasizing that designing a customized product to meet novel spatial, load, or architectural parameters does not constitute SR&ED when the underlying engineering principles belong to the existing body of standard mechanical engineering practice. The decision reinforces a crucial second-order compliance insight: complexity of integration and commercial customization are legally distinct from technological uncertainty, and the evidentiary burden rests squarely on the claimant to demonstrate why competent professionals in the relevant discipline could not resolve the system constraints using standard, established engineering methodologies.
Canafric Inc. v. The King (TCC)

Conversely, in Canafric Inc. v. The King, the Tax Court of Canada demonstrated that SR&ED eligibility is not restricted to high-technology laboratories or advanced software architectures, ruling that the experimental development of commercial food recipes and processing formulations qualified for SR&ED tax credits. When scaling food formulations from kitchen prototypes to industrial manufacturing lines introduced non-linear chemical and physical stability uncertainties that could not be predicted from standard food science literature, the taxpayer's systematic formulation of hypotheses, controlled batch testing, and analytical logging satisfied all five criteria of Northwest Hydraulic. Together, Joel Theatrical Rigging and Canafric illustrate that CRA technical reviewers cannot summarily approve or reject claims based on industry sector or perceived technological prestige; legal eligibility turns exclusively on the presence of genuine technological uncertainty and a documented, hypothesis-driven systematic investigation.
Federal Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and the 2024–2026 Reforms
Evolution from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Bill C-15

On December 16, 2024, the Department of Finance tabled the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), accompanied by a policy backgrounder titled Reforming and Enhancing the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. That initial December 2024 policy release proposed increasing the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $4,500,000, raising the prior-year taxable capital phase-out range from $10,000,000–$50,000,000 to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, extending the enhanced refundable credit to eligible Canadian public corporations, and restoring capital expenditure eligibility.

However, during subsequent legislative drafting and parliamentary enactment under Bill C-15—which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026—Parliament further increased the statutory expenditure limit to $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. The CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy confirms that for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the maximum expenditure limit is $3,000,000 (available solely to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations, or CCPCs), whereas for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum expenditure limit is $6,000,000 (available to both CCPCs and eligible Canadian public corporations). Consequently, an eligible CCPC or Canadian public corporation spending $6,000,000 on current SR&ED expenditures in a taxation year beginning on or after December 16, 2024 can generate up to $2,100,000 ($6,000,000 × 35%) in fully refundable federal ITCs—doubling the previous $1,050,000 maximum refundable federal entitlement.

body.text: Phase-Out Mechanics, Corporate Group Allocations, and Partnership Constraints

Under subsections 127(10.2) through 127(10.6) of the Income Tax Act, the annual expenditure limit ($3,000,000 for pre-December 16, 2024 taxation years; $6,000,000 for post-December 15, 2024 taxation years) must be shared among all corporations within an "associated group" as defined under section 256 of the Act. Associated corporations allocate the expenditure limit on Schedule 49 alongside their T2 returns and utilize Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) where intercompany assistance transfers occur. Furthermore, if a qualifying corporation has a short taxation year containing fewer than 365 days, its expenditure limit is prorated strictly by the ratio of the number of days in the taxation year to 365 under subsection 127(10.5). As illustrated in the CRA's Investment Tax Credit Policy, a corporation with a 184-day taxation year running from July 1 to December 31 has its baseline limit multiplied by 184/365, and specialized anti-duplication rules apply if a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated with another CCPC.

The statutory expenditure limit is subject to a straight-line phase-out based on corporate size metrics designed to target refundable support toward small and medium-sized scaling enterprises. For CCPCs, the expenditure limit decreases based on the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and its associated corporations for the preceding taxation year. Whereas the historical threshold began phasing out the expenditure limit once prior-year taxable capital reached $10,000,000 and eliminated it completely at $50,000,000, Bill C-15 elevated the phase-out corridor for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 to $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, respectively. Because publicly traded corporations frequently raise substantial equity capital on public exchanges before achieving commercial profitability, applying a taxable capital test to public companies would prematurely disqualify pre-revenue biotechnology or clean-tech issuers. To resolve this structural asymmetry, Bill C-15 introduced the statutory definition of an "eligible Canadian public corporation" under subsection 127(9) and implemented a phase-out tied to the corporation's average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years, as reflected in its audited financial statements. Where the public corporation is a member of a corporate group for the taxation year in question, the calculation requires aggregating the average annual financial statement revenue for each corporation in the group over the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether the corporations were associated during the entirety of that three-year window. Additionally, the legislative reforms provide qualifying optionality for CCPCs to elect between the taxable capital test and the revenue history metric where advantageous. Note also that under subsection 127.1(2), an "excluded corporation"—defined as a corporation that is, at any time in the year, controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more public corporations (other than an eligible Canadian public corporation or a prescribed venture capital corporation) or tax-exempt entities under section 149—cannot claim refundable ITCs on expenditures above the expenditure limit. Similarly, where SR&ED is prosecuted through a partnership under subsections 127(8) to 127(8.5), the partnership computes its notional qualified expenditure pool and allocates the resulting ITC to its members, but allocations to limited partners are strictly constrained by their "at-risk amount" under subsections 96(2.2) and 96(2.4), and partnership ITCs remain ineligible for the enhanced 35% CCPC rate.
Carryback, Carryforward, and Deemed Deduction Rules

Under subsection 127(5) and subsection 127(9), non-refundable SR&ED ITCs (or refundable ITCs that a claimant elects not to receive as a cash refund) first offset federal Part I income tax otherwise payable in the current taxation year. Any unused ITC balance remaining at year-end may be carried back up to three preceding taxation years to recover previously paid Part I tax, or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years. Certain informal practitioner summaries erroneously cite a 10-year carryforward period; this reflects obsolete law, as the federal statutory carryforward period under subsection 127(9) is strictly 20 years, matching the 20-year ITC recapture window under subsection 127(27).

Under subsection 127.1(3) of the Income Tax Act, any SR&ED ITC refunded in cash to a claimant in a taxation year is statutorily deemed to have been deducted under subsection 127(5) against Part I tax otherwise payable in that year. Consequently, a cash refund immediately extinguishes that portion of the ITC pool so it cannot be carried forward or back, and simultaneously triggers an inclusion in the taxpayer's taxable income (or a reduction of the subsection 37(1) deductible SR&ED expenditure pool) in the subsequent taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(t) and paragraph 37(1)(e) of the Act. Furthermore, if a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (a change of control), strict loss-streaming restrictions under subsection 37(6.1) and subsection 127(9.1) restrict the deductibility of the pre-acquisition subsection 37(1) expenditure pool and the carryforward of unused ITCs to income generated from the same or a similar business.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies

To generate an Investment Tax Credit, an outlay must first constitute an allowable SR&ED expenditure under section 37 and subsequently meet the definition of a "qualified expenditure" under subsection 127(9). Claimants report allowable expenditures in Part 3 of Form T661 (culminating at Line 380 for current and capital allowable expenditures, and Line 455 for the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures) and compute total qualified SR&ED expenditures in Part 4 of Form T661 (Line 570).
Salaries and Wages and the Specified Employee Restrictions

Salaries and wages paid to employees who are directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada constitute the primary expenditure category under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) and Regulation 2900(2). Eligible remuneration includes gross base wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, and sick leave, provided the expenditure is incurred in the year and unpaid remuneration is actually paid within 180 days after the end of the taxation year pursuant to subsection 78(4) and subsection 127(26) of the Income Tax Act.

However, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations enforce stringent anti-avoidance caps on "specified employees"—defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who is a specified shareholder (owning, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation) or who does not deal at arm's length with the employer. For specified employees, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits are strictly excluded from allowable SR&ED salaries and wages, and the maximum directly claimable SR&ED salary of a specified employee cannot exceed five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days the individual was employed in the taxation year.

Even more restrictive is the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Cap under Regulation 2900(7). When a claimant elects the Proxy Method to compute overhead, the amount of a specified employee's salary that may be included in the salary base for the 55% PPA calculation is constrained by Regulation 2900(7) to the least of three statutory figures: the actual SR&ED portion of the specified employee's eligible base salary; 75% of the specified employee's total salary and wages (excluding bonuses and taxable benefits) from the employer for the year; and 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year in which the individual was employed by the taxpayer. Where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, the maximum salary limits must be allocated across the associated group using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)). Because early-stage technical founders are almost universally specified employees, failing to pay founders via regular T4 payroll—or compensating them via dividends or year-end bonuses—permanently forfeits both the direct wage credit and the 55% proxy overhead uplift.
Overhead Calculation: Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

Taxpayers must make an irrevocable annual election on Form T661 for each taxation year to calculate SR&ED overhead using either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method. Under the Proxy Method, codified in subsection 127(9) and Regulation 2900(4), the taxpayer avoids the administrative burden of tracking and substantiating individual shop-floor overhead invoices by calculating a notional overhead figure—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—equal to 55% of the eligible salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (subject to the Regulation 2900(7) cap for specified employees). The PPA is not added to the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible expenditures—because actual overhead costs such as office supplies, clerical support, and utilities are already deducted as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the Income Tax Act—but the PPA is added directly to "qualified expenditures" on Form T661 to earn the 15% or 35% SR&ED ITC.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, no notional proxy is claimed. Instead, the taxpayer must specifically identify, substantiate, and allocate actual overhead and other expenditures that are "directly related" and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada under Regulation 2900(2)(c) and 2900(3). While the Traditional Method allows non-direct SR&ED employer-paid payroll burdens and dedicated facility overheads to enter both the subsection 37(1) deduction pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure base directly, the granular invoice-level substantiation demanded during a CRA financial review renders the Proxy Method vastly superior for labour-intensive R&D performers.
Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, Materials, and Cloud Computing

Beyond internal labour and overhead, subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) govern third-party and material outlays across several distinct statutory tracks. Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and paragraph (a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), payments made to arm's-length subcontractors to perform SR&ED in Canada on behalf of the claimant are 100% deductible in the section 37 pool, but only 80% of the contract expenditure enters the qualified expenditure pool to earn the ITC. This 20% statutory haircut (enacted in 2013 under Bill C-45) is designed to strip out the subcontractor's presumed commercial profit margin. Where the subcontractor does not deal at arm's length with the claimant, paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) bars the payer from claiming an ITC on the contract payment; instead, the non-arm's-length performer must either claim the underlying SR&ED costs directly or transfer the qualified expenditures to the payer by filing Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length). Similarly, "third-party payments" made under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) to (iii) to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit SR&ED corporations for SR&ED carried on in Canada that relates to the claimant's business (and which the claimant is entitled to exploit) are 80% included in qualified expenditures and must be reported on Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED).

Materials consumed (rendered virtually valueless) or transformed (integrated into an experimental prototype or pilot plant) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada qualify at 100% under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) and Regulation 2900(2)(a). In the context of modern software, artificial intelligence, and data science R&D, cloud computing and data processing expenses (such as dedicated AWS, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud GPU clusters) qualify for SR&ED only to the extent that the computing instances are directly attributable and dedicated to eligible experimental development or model training. Claimants must segregate development and experimental training environments from commercial production hosting, as CRA financial reviewers strictly disallow multi-purpose or commercial SaaS hosting invoices that lack clear allocation telemetry.

body.text: The Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Shared-Use Equipment (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures (and lease costs for capital property) were completely excluded from both the section 37 deduction pool and the section 127 ITC calculation following the legislative repeal enacted by the Jobs and Growth Act, 2012 (Bill C-45). Effective for property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 (and, in the case of lease costs, amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024), Bill C-15 fully restored the eligibility of capital expenditures under rules mirroring the pre-2014 statutory regime.

As set out in the CRA's updated Shared-Use Equipment Policy and Investment Tax Credit Policy, restored capital eligibility bifurcates into two distinct statutory tracks. Under the first track—All or Substantially All (ASA) SR&ED Capital Property governed by paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127(9)—depreciable property qualifies for 100% inclusion in the section 37 deduction pool and 100% inclusion in qualified expenditures for the ITC if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant's demonstrated intention is either to use the property during all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in SR&ED activities carried out in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of the property's value in the prosecution of SR&ED carried out in Canada. The cost of capital property is determined without taking into account the cost of borrowed money, without reference to deemed capital cost provisions, and after adjustments for non-arm's-length transfers under subsection 127(11.6) (which was repealed on February 1, 2017, and formally reintroduced on December 16, 2024).

Under the second track—First-Term and Second-Term Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) governed by subsection 127(9)—manufacturing and engineering firms that acquire multi-purpose machinery used partly for R&D and partly for commercial production can earn partial ITCs. To qualify as first-term SUE, the asset must be new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024; must not qualify as 90% ASA capital property; must not be "prescribed depreciable property" (PDP—defined as property where the claimant intended at the time of acquisition that it would be used primarily for non-SR&ED purposes over its expected useful life, or that its value would be consumed primarily in non-SR&ED activities); must not be "general purpose office equipment or furniture" (GPOEF); and must actually be used primarily (more than 50% of operating time) for SR&ED in Canada during the "first period". If these cumulative conditions are satisfied, 25% of the capital cost qualifies for the ITC as first-term SUE, and if primary SR&ED usage continues through the "second period," an additional 25% of the capital cost qualifies as second-term SUE, yielding a cumulative 50% qualified expenditure inclusion. For instance, if a corporation acquires eligible new equipment for $300,000 and satisfies the first-term SUE requirements, $75,000 (25% × $300,000) is included as a qualified expenditure for calculating the ITC, and any ITC earned and applied to reduce taxes payable or refunded reduces the undepreciated capital cost (UCC) of the asset's Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) class in the subsequent taxation year.
The 20-Year ITC Recapture Regime Under Subsections 127(27) to 127(36)

Whenever a claimant earns an SR&ED ITC on tangible property—including materials transformed into a custom product, a commercial asset, experimental production, or commercial production with experimental development; animals and other growing things used in SR&ED projects; ASA capital equipment; shared-use equipment; or property acquired through a contract involving SR&ED—the property becomes subject to the Recapture of Investment Tax Credit rules under subsections 127(27) through 127(36) of the Income Tax Act.

If, within 20 taxation years of the original expenditure, the claimant disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use (determined by reference to the available-for-use rules under subsection 13(27)), the previously claimed ITC is recaptured and added directly to the taxpayer's federal Part I tax payable on Line 602 of the T2 return via Schedule 31. Under subsection 127(27) and paragraph 127(27)(d), the recaptured tax is equal to the lesser of the actual amount of the SR&ED ITC originally earned on the property, and the ITC percentage applied to the proceeds of disposition (if sold to an arm's-length party) or the fair market value of the property at the time of disposition or conversion to commercial use (if converted internally or transferred to a non-arm's-length party). For example, if a CCPC claims a 35% ITC on $300,000 of expenditures ($105,000 ITC), of which $135,000 represents materials transformed into an experimental prototype that is later converted to commercial use, the recapture triggered on conversion is $47,250 (35% × $135,000). For shared-use equipment, recapture is triggered after the first period only when the property is sold or when all or substantially all of the property has been converted to commercial use (meaning SR&ED usage becomes merely incidental), and only the SUE inclusion percentage (25% for first-term only, or 50% for first- and second-term SUE) of the proceeds of disposition or fair market value is multiplied by the ITC rate. Thus, if equipment that earned $28,000 of ITCs across first- and second-term SUE at a 35% rate is later sold for $100,000, the recapture is the lesser of $28,000 and $17,500 (35% × 50% × $100,000).

A critical second-order audit insight highlighted in Section 7.1 of the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy governs the disparate treatment of externally purchased versus internally manufactured SR&ED components. If a claimant contracts an arm's-length supplier for $12,000 to manufacture and develop a specialized component ($10,000 manufacturing and development cost plus a $2,000 profit element), the entire $12,000 cost of the acquired property is subject to recapture under subsections 127(27) and 127(32) if the resulting unit is subsequently commercialized. Conversely, if the claimant manufactures that exact same part in-house using its own employees, there is no recapture on the internal salaries or overhead costs used to manufacture the part; only the raw material cost is exposed to recapture. Similarly, where intellectual property (IP) belongs to the payer ab initio under the terms of an R&D contract, the payer is not acquiring physical property; the IP simply accrues to the payer as it is generated, meaning that selling or commercializing the IP never triggers ITC recapture.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Stacking Mechanics

In addition to the federal SR&ED program, Canadian provinces and the Yukon Territory offer supplementary R&D tax credits that rely on the federal technical definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1). Under subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(18) of the federal Income Tax Act, provincial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance". Consequently, any provincial R&D tax credit earned in a taxation year (unless formally renounced or waived by the taxpayer within the statutory deadline) reduces the federal pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and reduces the federal qualified expenditure base prior to applying the 15% or 35% federal ITC rate.

body.text: Deep-Dive: Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) and Bill C-15 Technical Reconciliation

Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), enacted under Sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (and detailed in Information Circular IEG-1) for eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020, employs a unique two-tier incremental architecture rather than the flat percentage rate used in Ontario (8% OITC / 3.5% ORDTC) or British Columbia (10%). Claimed directly on AT1 Schedule 29 alongside the Alberta corporate income tax return within 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing due date, the IEG provides an 8% base payment on current-year eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to the corporation's "base level of spending" (determined by calculating the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding two taxation years) and an enhanced 20% payment (comprising the 8% base rate plus a 12% incremental enhancement) on eligible R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's two-year historical base level, up to a combined annual eligible expenditure limit of $4,000,000. The IEG phases out incrementally for firms with between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 in taxable capital and is unavailable to firms with $50,000,000 or more in taxable capital.

To illustrate the two-tier mechanics and cap interaction, consider a corporation with an Alberta permanent establishment that incurred $1,200,000 of eligible Alberta R&D expenditures in Year 1 and $1,800,000 in Year 2, establishing a two-year average baseline of $1,500,000. If the corporation incurs $3,000,000 of eligible Alberta R&D expenditures in Year 3, the first $1,500,000 (at or below the baseline) earns 8% ($120,000), while the incremental $1,500,000 (above the baseline) earns 20% ($300,000), generating a total refundable IEG entitlement of $420,000. If the same corporation instead spends $4,000,000 (or more) in Year 3, the first $1,500,000 of the $4,000,000 cap is absorbed by the 8% baseline rate ($120,000) and only the remaining $2,500,000 headroom within the $4,000,000 cap earns the 20% incremental rate ($500,000), producing a maximum cap-constrained credit of $620,000—below the theoretical $800,000 headline maximum (20% × $4,000,000) that would only be achievable if the prior two-year baseline were zero.

A critical post-Bill C-15 compliance anomaly requires careful attention when preparing AT1 Schedule 29. Because Bill C-15 restored capital expenditures to federal Form T661 for taxation years ending after December 15, 2024, Line 559 of Form T661 now includes capital expenditures. In corporate tax software packages, Line 559 of Form T661 historically flowed directly to Line 003 on the AS29Step worksheet (and Columns 105, 107, and 111 of the AS29Project list table). To prevent federal capital expenditures from improperly appearing on AT1 Schedule 29, the line-reference rule requires using Line 559 of Form T661 for taxation years ending before December 16, 2024, but overriding to use Line 557 of Form T661 for taxation years ending after December 15, 2024. Similarly, practitioners must note that provincial regimes do not automatically mirror the federal $6,000,000 expenditure limit expansion; Manitoba's 15% credit on Schedule 380 does not use the federal enhanced limit, Ontario's OITC remains capped at $3,000,000 (phasing out between $500,000 and $800,000 of prior-year federal taxable income or $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 of specified capital), and Saskatchewan specifically doubled its CCPC refundable R&D credit threshold on Schedule 403 from $1,000,000 to $2,000,000 effective December 16, 2024, while maintaining a $1,000,000 total annual credit cap.
Direct Grant Stacking and the Section 127(18) Government Assistance Grind

Canadian R&D performers frequently stack non-dilutive direct government grants and conditionally repayable contributions with federal and provincial SR&ED tax credits—with 70% of Alberta SR&ED claimants utilizing at least one additional funding program. The principal federal and regional direct funding instruments include the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which provides up to $1,000,000 in non-repayable contributions per project for eligible internal technical wages and Canadian subcontractor costs; PrairiesCan Business Scale-up and Productivity (BSP) and PacifiCan / ACOA Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative (RAII), which provide $200,000 to $5,000,000 in interest-free conditionally repayable contributions; Alberta Innovates vouchers (covering 75% of eligible project costs up to $100,000 for TRL 4–9) and AICE grants (up to $300,000–$600,000 at 75% cost share); Emissions Reduction Alberta (ERA) grants ($500,000 to $15,000,000 for clean technology transformation); and CanExport Innovation (75% of eligible costs up to $37,500 per project, capped at $100,000 per 12 months).

Under subsection 127(18) of the Income Tax Act, any government assistance received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received reduces the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool dollar-for-dollar before provincial and federal tax credits are calculated. Despite this anti-double-dipping reduction, stacking a direct grant with SR&ED and provincial credits yields substantially higher total non-dilutive capital recovery than claiming SR&ED alone. For example, if a CCPC spends $500,000 on eligible R&D and claims only SR&ED (at 35% = $175,000) and the 8% base Alberta IEG ($40,000), its total recovery is $215,000. If the same CCPC secures a $200,000 NRC IRAP grant covering wages, its SR&ED and IEG qualified expenditure pool is reduced from $500,000 to $300,000, generating $105,000 in federal SR&ED credits (35% × $300,000) and $24,000 in base IEG (8% × $300,000), for a combined funding recovery of $329,000 ($200,000 IRAP + $129,000 tax credits). Where an Alberta CCPC with $600,000 in total R&D spend ($200,000 of which is incremental above its two-year average) stacks a $200,000 IRAP grant with the 20% incremental IEG ($40,000), 8% base IEG ($16,000), and 35% federal SR&ED ($140,000), total funding recovery reaches $396,000, representing an effective recovery rate of 66% of total R&D spend.

body.text: Administrative Compliance, Statutory Deadlines, and CRA Audit Defence
Required Tax Forms and Statutory Filing Deadlines

The Canada Revenue Agency enforces an absolute statutory bar on late-filed SR&ED claims. A complete SR&ED claim requires the submission of the current version of Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim)—which captures the technical narrative for each project in Part 2, allowable expenditures in Part 3, and qualified expenditure calculations in Part 4—together with Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) for corporate claimants or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit – Individuals) for individuals and unincorporated businesses, plus any applicable auxiliary schedules (Form T1145, Form T1146, Form T1174, and Form T1263).

The statutory SR&ED reporting deadline is strictly 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred. Because the Income Tax Act requires a taxable corporation to file its T2 Corporation Income Tax Return within 6 months after the end of its taxation year, a corporation's absolute SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of its taxation year (6 months + 12 months). For example, a corporation with a December 31, 2024 taxation year-end has a T2 filing due date of June 30, 2025, and an absolute SR&ED reporting deadline of June 30, 2026. If a claimant fails to report its projects and prescribed expenditures on Form T661 and Schedule 31 on or before the 18-month deadline, the CRA has no statutory authority to grant extensions, and the unclaimed expenditures and ITCs are permanently lost. Different statutory filing windows apply to other taxpayer categories: a tax-exempt corporation that incurs SR&ED expenditures must file Form T661 on or before its T2 return due date (6 months after its taxation year-end) to avoid a late-filing penalty; a trust must file within 12 months after its T3 return due date (which falls 90 days after the trust's taxation year-end); and an individual carrying on an unincorporated business must file within 12 months after their T1 return due date of June 15 (i.e., by June 15 of the following calendar year).
Part 9 Claim Preparer Disclosures and the Subsection 162(5.1) Penalty

To monitor contingency-fee arrangements and enforce accountability among external R&D consultants, Parliament enacted subsection 162(5.1) of the Income Tax Act, operationalized through Part 9 of Form T661 (Claim preparer information). Every corporate or individual claimant must complete Part 9 to disclose whether a prescribed claim preparer participated in preparing the claim, detailing the preparer's identity, billing arrangement, and fee structure. If a claim preparer did not prepare or assist in the preparation of Form T661, the claimant must still complete Lines 935, 970, and 975 in Part 9 to certify in-house preparation, whereas if multiple claim preparers assisted, a separate Form T661 Part 9 must be submitted for each preparer. If complete and accurate claim preparer information is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, subsection 162(5.1) imposes a $1,000 penalty, for which the taxpayer and the claim preparer may be assessed.
CRA Review Workflows, Risk Assessment Systems, and Service Standards

Because Forms T661, T2SCH31, T2038(IND), T1174, T1145, T1146, and T1263 form an integral part of the income tax return, all submissions are received at CRA Tax Centres and processed through the CORTAX system for corporations (or stored in Integras for T1 claims). SR&ED technical and financial field staff access CORTAX to perform detailed risk assessments and record audit actions within the Audit Information Management System (AIMS).

The CRA adheres to published service standards depending on the review pathway selected by its risk-assessment algorithms. Complete refundable claims that are accepted as filed without review are processed within a service standard of 60 calendar days from receipt (with 90% of unreviewed claims meeting this benchmark). Claims that have undergone the CRA's formal pre-claim approval process and are subsequently selected for review carry a 90-calendar-day service standard. Standard refundable claims selected for technical and financial review carry a service standard of 180 calendar days from the receipt of a complete claim, while claims submitted via an amended T2 return typically require between 180 and 240 days to process.

During a CRA review, claimants must be prepared to sit for technical interviews and provide contemporaneous documentation—created naturally during the progression of the R&D rather than reconstructed in arrears—to substantiate both the technological narrative and the underlying financial ledger. Retrospective reconstruction of project narratives after the taxation year has closed is the single largest cause of audit denials. An audit-resilient compliance file integrates patent and literature benchmark searches, dated hypothesis logs, version-control commit notes or Slack/sprint summaries capturing failed experimental iterations, laboratory notebooks, contemporaneous employee time-tracking logs, and general ledger reconciliations tying payroll, subcontractor statements of work, and dedicated cloud computing invoices directly to Part 3 of Form T661.
Strategic Synthesis and Compliance Recommendations

The structural transformation of the Canadian SR&ED regime enacted through Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 fundamentally reshapes capital budgeting, corporate structuring, and multi-jurisdictional tax planning for innovative enterprises operating in Canada.

First, capital-intensive R&D performers must immediately re-engineer their capital procurement and equipment tracking protocols to capture the restored eligibility of 90% all-or-substantially-all (ASA) capital property under paragraph 37(1)(b) and 25%/50% shared-use equipment (SUE) under subsection 127(9) for depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024. Because an asset is permanently disqualified from SUE if it is classified as Prescribed Depreciable Property (where the taxpayer's long-term intention at acquisition is primarily commercial use), capital requisition files and board resolutions must contemporaneously document the intention to utilize new multi-purpose equipment primarily (more than 50%) for SR&ED during the first and second operating periods, supported by machine-hour operating logs.

Second, scaling CCPCs with prior-year taxable capital between $10,000,000 and $75,000,000—many of which were previously phased out of the enhanced refundable credit—should re-model their associated-group expenditure limit allocations to take full advantage of the doubled $6,000,000 expenditure ceiling and the widened $15,000,000–$75,000,000 taxable capital phase-out corridor. Concurrently, publicly traded Canadian technology and life sciences issuers must compile three-year consolidated financial statement revenue histories to claim the newly extended 35% refundable ITC as eligible Canadian public corporations under subsection 127(9).

Third, CCPC founders and shareholder-executives performing hands-on technical R&D must structure their compensation as regular periodic T4 base salary rather than dividends or performance bonuses, ensuring compliance with the 180-day payment rule and maximizing the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount within the strict Regulation 2900(7) cap, while filing Form T1174 whenever specified employee services span associated corporations.

Fourth, multi-provincial claimants must sequence direct grants (such as NRC IRAP and Alberta Innovates) and provincial tax credits ahead of the federal ITC calculation to accurately account for the subsection 127(18) government assistance grind. In Alberta, tax preparers completing AT1 Schedule 29 (AS29Step Line 003 and AS29Project) for taxation years ending after December 15, 2024 must map to Line 557 (rather than Line 559) of federal Form T661 so that restored federal capital expenditures do not contaminate the provincial IEG calculation. Simultaneously, Saskatchewan CCPCs should leverage the doubled $2,000,000 refundable expenditure ceiling on Schedule 403, while Manitoba claimants unable to absorb the 7.5% non-refundable half of the Manitoba R&D credit should evaluate formal renunciation on Schedule 380 within 6 months of taxation year-end to preserve their federal SR&ED qualified expenditure base.

Finally, to insulate claims against CRA technical and financial review under Northwest Hydraulic and Joel Theatrical Rigging, engineering teams must embed contemporaneous hypothesis-test-result logging into daily development workflows. When engaging arm's-length Canadian subcontractors, agreements should explicitly stipulate that SR&ED is performed on behalf of the claimant in Canada and that all resulting IP vests ab initio in the payer, while recognizing that physical prototype components manufactured in-house avoid the full-cost subsection 127(27) ITC recapture exposure that attaches to externally purchased assemblies upon future commercialization.
